newsitem.title: UK: Britain to go ahead with mad cow cattle cull.
newsitem.headline: Britain to go ahead with mad cow cattle cull.

text.p: Britain, in a major u-turn, announced on Monday it would slaughter around 100,000 more cattle in a bid to persuade the European Union to lift its worldwide ban on British beef exports.

A selective cull was agreed by Prime Minister John Major with other EU heads of government at the Florence European summit last June as part of a package to end the crisis over mad cow disease. But he scrapped the plan in September.
"We have decided that now is the time to bring forward our proposals for a selective cull in accordance with the terms of the Florence agreement," Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg told parliament.
"We regard this as only the first step towards the complete lifting of the ban on the export of cattle, beef and beef products from the UK."
But the selective cull of animals most at risk of BSE would not lead to a quick resumption of British exports, he said.

"We will now pursue discussions in Brussels as rapidly as possible, of course. That process may take longer than we would wish." Hogg made his statement before flying to Brussels for an EU farm ministers meeting on Tuesday.

The EU imposed a ban on beef exports in March after the British government disclosed that the disease, known medically as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), could spread to people who ate infected beef and lead to a fatal brain disease.
But Britain said in September it was suspending the scheme after fresh scientific evidence suggested that BSE would be eradicated by the year 2001 under existing measures.

The EU has however made clear there could be no progress on raising the export ban until the cull was carried out. After the Florence summit, Major had said he expected the beef ban could begin to be lifted in November.
On Monday EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler was cautious about any lifting of the ban on British beef exports, despite the extra slaughter plans.
"I think we need to move forward step by step as agreed," he told a Brussels news conference.

Hogg said he could not be certain how many cattle would now need to be slaughtered under the selective cull, which would come on top of the one million cattle older than 30 months already slaughtered in Britain in response to the mad cow scare.

He said the government's original estimate of 128,000 cattle was out of date, as many of these animals would have been already slaughtered. But if 100,000 were slaughtered, the cost could be up to 150 million pounds ($250 million).

The government says a selective cull is not scientifically necessary to combat mad cow disease but believes it would put the onus on other European nations to honour their side of the agreement made at the Florence summit.

Political sources said they hoped that the decision to go ahead with at least part of the cull would in turn pave the way for the lifting of an export ban on so-called "certified herds" -- BSE-free, grass-fed cattle mostly found in Northern Ireland and Scotland. ($1=.6027 Pound)
